title: A principled closure framework for higher-order SIS epidemic models on networks
authors: Kevin Teo, Peter L Simon, István Zoltán Kiss
abstract: Susceptible-infected-susceptible (SIS) epidemic models on networks are governed by hierarchical moment equations where the dynamics of smaller subsystems depend on the state of larger ones. Moment closure approximations, which truncate this hierarchy by expressing higher-order state probabilities in terms of lower-order ones, are essential for obtaining tractable reduced systems. Higher-order networks, which extend the pairwise structure to include group interactions, introduce a combinatorial explosion of closure configurations, making systematic derivation harder. Consequently, existing higher-order SIS models are derived heuristically, where structural and dynamical assumptions underpinning their closures are not always apparent from the formulation alone. We develop a bottom-up derivation of higher-order SIS dynamics, building systematically from node-level equations to pairs, triplets, and three-body interactions. Central to our approach is a network-dependent closure operator that generates topologically appropriate approximations from local pairwise and triadic structure. Using this framework, we recover three existing higher-order SIS models--Burgio et al.'s maximal clique, Malizia et al.'s pair-based and inter-order models--as special cases, each arising under specific topological and dynamical assumptions. Our derivation reveals assumptions that are invisible from heuristic approaches: for instance, Malizia et al.'s inter-order overlap parameter is insufficient alone to express the model within our framework despite performing well against simulations, with the original derivation implicitly invoking additional structural assumptions. Our framework offers both a foundation for higher-order epidemic modeling and a constructive pathway for understanding the assumptions implicit in heuristically derived mean-field closures and provides a principled method of generating new models.
summary: This work introduces a rigorous, bottom-up framework for modeling epidemic spread (SIS) on networks that include group interactions via hyperedges. It systematically derives the necessary moment equations and provides a principled closure operator to manage the resulting mathematical complexity. The paper is significant because it moves beyond heuristic approximations by explicitly quantifying the underlying structural assumptions required in mean-field descriptions of complex interacting systems.
main_problem: The paper develops a principled, systematic framework for deriving mean-field approximations for higher-order Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) epidemic models on complex networks.
main_result: It establishes a network-dependent closure operator that rigorously derives higher-order dynamics and explicitly reveals the often-unstated structural and dynamical assumptions underlying existing heuristic epidemic models.
method: The methodology involves deriving coupled rate equations for increasing moments (up to triplets) of the system state, followed by systematically truncating the resulting moment hierarchy using topological constraints and closure operators.
model_or_system: The model is an SIS epidemic process occurring on a higher-order network structure defined by nodes, pairwise edges ($E$), and hyperedges ($H$). The dynamics are governed by continuous-time Markov chain rate equations.
key_observables: State probabilities (e.g., $\langle I_i angle$, $\langle S_i I_j angle$, $\langle S_i S_j I_k angle$), motif densities, and global network parameters like the clustering coefficient ($\phi$).
important_parameters: Infection rates ($ eta_1$ for edges, $ eta_2$ for hyperedges) and recovery rate ($\gamma$). The analysis depends on local and global topological descriptors.
main_assumptions: The framework relies on truncating the moment hierarchy at the triplet level. Specific derivations assume dynamical homogeneity (Assumption 5.1), topological homogeneity (Assumption 5.2), and strong sparsity conditions to simplify complex motif contributions.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first establishing the microscopic rate equations for low-order moments, then systematically introducing the closure problem due to hierarchical coupling. It develops the network-dependent closure operator through bottom-up derivation, culminating in detailed term-by-term derivations showing how higher-order contributions simplify under specific assumptions.
why_interesting: While focused on epidemiology, the mathematical machinery—developing systematic closures for high-dimensional moment equations based on local topology and combinatorial identities—is directly analogous to techniques used in analyzing complex interacting quantum systems or many-body physics models where exact solutions are intractable.
